title: dbt vs Dataflow Gen2 vs Spark Notebooks vs Stored Procedures
purpose: Decide which Fabric transformation surface owns a given piece of logic — SQL-first version-controlled modelling, low-code ingestion/shaping, Spark-shaped non-tabular work, or embedded procedural T-SQL — instead of splitting one logical transformation layer across tools that can't see each other.
accessibleSummary: A decision tree rooted at 'what kind of transformation work is this?'. Three branches: version-controlled, tested SQL modelling of already-landed data routes to dbt against the Warehouse via the third-party dbt-fabric adapter; low-code ingestion and shaping for analysts routes to Dataflow Gen2; Python/Spark work over Lakehouse/OneLake data routes to notebooks. A fourth node covers Warehouse stored procedures as the fallback when no external tooling is wanted. A warning node flags the T-SQL surface limits every dbt model inherits, and a second warning flags the anti-pattern of splitting one transformation layer across two tools.
longDescription: This is a decision tree, not a pipeline. The root question is what kind of transformation work needs to happen and on which side of the lake/warehouse boundary the data already sits. Choosing SQL-first, version-controlled, tested modelling of data already landed in a Warehouse routes to dbt, which reaches Fabric only through the community/Microsoft-maintained dbt-fabric PyPI adapter — not a native Fabric feature — installed and run from outside Fabric (VS Code/CLI) against the SQL analytics endpoint. Choosing low-code, connector-driven ingestion and shaping for analysts routes to Dataflow Gen2. Choosing Python/Scala transformation over Lakehouse/OneLake data, unstructured work, or ML feature engineering routes to Spark notebooks. A fourth path is Warehouse stored procedures for teams that want transformation logic embedded directly in T-SQL without external tooling. Two warning nodes matter: dbt-fabric compensates for T-SQL commands Fabric Warehouse doesn't support (ALTER, MERGE, TRUNCATE, sp_rename) by generating CREATE TABLE AS SELECT plus DROP/CREATE sequences, which has cost and behavioural implications; and splitting one logical transformation layer across two tools loses the lineage and testing benefits dbt exists to provide.

nodes.label: What kind of transformation is this?
nodes.summary: Root question: version-controlled SQL modelling, low-code shaping, Spark-shaped work, or embedded T-SQL.
nodes.detail: Fabric offers several transformation surfaces that overlap in capability but differ in skillset, tooling location, and target engine. Before picking one, name what the work actually is: is it modelling already-landed warehouse data with tests and lineage, is it low-code ingestion/shaping for an analyst, is it Python/Spark work over lake data, or is it procedural T-SQL a team wants to keep entirely inside the Warehouse.
nodes.whyItMatters: Picking the tool before naming the work is how teams end up with one logical transformation layer split across two surfaces that can't see each other's lineage or tests.

inputs: The transformation requirement in plain language
Where the source data currently lives (Warehouse vs Lakehouse/OneLake)
Whether tests, lineage, and code review are a stated requirement
processing: State whether the target of the write is the Warehouse or the Lakehouse
Decide whether version control and automated testing are required for this layer
Identify who will own and maintain the logic day to day
outputs: A routed decision into one of the four transformation-surface branches
drill.example: A team standing up a tested, version-controlled star schema on top of already-landed Warehouse silver tables identifies this as SQL-first modelling with lineage requirements, routing toward dbt rather than a dataflow or notebook.
controls: Write down the target engine and the testing requirement before picking a tool
failureModes: Picking a tool by team familiarity rather than the actual shape of the work
Letting analysts and engineers each build a parallel transformation layer for the same data because nobody named the boundary

nodes.label: dbt (via dbt-fabric adapter)
nodes.summary: SQL-first, version-controlled, tested modelling inside Fabric Warehouse via a third-party PyPI adapter.
nodes.detail: dbt targets Fabric Warehouse through the dbt-fabric adapter, a Python package installed with `pip install dbt-fabric`, not a Fabric-native integration. It is driven from outside Fabric — VS Code or CLI — requiring Python, the Microsoft ODBC Driver for SQL Server, and a SQL analytics endpoint connection string in profiles.yml. Its unit of work is the model; its output is warehouse tables and views with version control, automated tests, and lineage as first-class citizens.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the right choice when a team brings an existing dbt practice or specifically wants tests, lineage, and code review on the modelled, tested semantic-ready layer — capabilities the other three surfaces don't provide natively.

evidence.note: Fabric Data Warehouse is supported as a dbt target via the dbt-fabric adapter, a Python package published on PyPI and installed with `pip install dbt-fabric`, rather than through a Fabric-native dbt integration.

A dbt project connects to Fabric Warehouse through a profiles.yml output block that sets type: fabric, the SQL analytics endpoint host, database/schema names, an ODBC driver string, and an authentication mode.

inputs: Already-landed silver data in a Fabric Warehouse (or reachable via cross-database three-part names from a lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint)
A dbt project with models, tests, and a profiles.yml pointing at the warehouse
processing: Install the dbt-fabric adapter and configure profiles.yml with type: fabric and the SQL analytics endpoint host
Author models as SQL SELECT statements with ref()/source() dependencies
Run dbt debug/seed/run/test to validate connectivity and materialize models as warehouse tables/views
outputs: Tested, version-controlled warehouse tables and views with dbt-generated lineage documentation
drill.example: A team builds a star schema gold layer in wh_gold from silver tables in lakehouse lh_analytics, referencing the lakehouse through cross-database three-part names, with relationship and grain tests defined per model.
controls: Choice of Entra ID auth mode (CLI for developers, service principal for CI/production)
Which models are materialized as tables vs views
failureModes: Assuming dbt is a first-party Fabric feature and expecting Fabric-native scheduling or support
Targeting a Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint expecting writes — it is read-only for T-SQL, so dbt cannot materialize tables there

nodes.label: Dataflow Gen2 (Power Query)
nodes.summary: Low-code ingestion and shaping for analysts, strongest for connector breadth and landing data into Fabric.
nodes.detail: Dataflow Gen2 is Fabric's low-code, Power Query-based ingestion and shaping surface, aimed at analysts and connector-heavy source integration rather than a large interdependent transformation codebase. It is the tool for landing data into Fabric with minimal code, not for owning a tested, version-controlled modelling layer.
nodes.whyItMatters: It fills a different niche than dbt: fast, low-code connectivity and shaping for an analyst audience, at the cost of the version control, testing, and lineage rigor dbt provides for a modelling layer.

inputs: Source connections via Power Query connectors
Analyst-authored shaping steps (filters, joins, type conversions)
processing: Connect to sources through Power Query's connector library
Apply low-code transformation steps in the Dataflow Gen2 editor
Land the shaped output into a Fabric destination (lakehouse, warehouse, or external)
outputs: Shaped, landed data ready for downstream consumption or further modelling
drill.example: An analyst ingests a CRM export and a spreadsheet of budget targets, joins and reshapes them with Power Query steps, and lands the result into a lakehouse table for a Spark notebook to conform further.
controls: Which connector and refresh cadence is used per source
Whether the dataflow output feeds a downstream dbt or notebook stage rather than being treated as a final model
failureModes: Using Dataflow Gen2 to own a large, interdependent transformation codebase it wasn't designed for, losing maintainability as step counts grow
Building modelling logic in a dataflow that a downstream dbt project can't see, fragmenting lineage

nodes.label: Spark notebooks
nodes.summary: Python/Scala transformation over Lakehouse/OneLake data, unstructured work, and ML feature engineering.
nodes.detail: Spark notebooks handle Python/Scala transformations over Lakehouse and OneLake data, unstructured or semi-structured work, and ML feature engineering — work that operates on the lake side rather than through the warehouse's T-SQL endpoint. They are the right surface when the work outgrows what SQL comfortably expresses.
nodes.whyItMatters: Notebooks are the only one of the four surfaces built for non-tabular data and general-purpose Python/Scala logic; routing SQL-shaped modelling work here instead of to dbt or stored procedures forces awkward SQL-in-Spark patterns.

inputs: Raw or semi-structured data in Lakehouse Files/Tables or OneLake
Python/Scala transformation logic, potentially including ML feature engineering
processing: Read source data with Spark DataFrame APIs or Spark SQL
Apply transformation, feature engineering, or unstructured-data parsing logic in Python/Scala
Write conformed output back to Lakehouse Delta tables
outputs: Conformed Delta tables or ML feature sets in the lakehouse
drill.example: A notebook parses semi-structured JSON event logs, extracts and casts fields, and writes a conformed bronze-to-silver table — a shape of work dbt's SQL-only models can't express directly.
controls: Choice of Spark pool sizing and autoscale settings
Whether the notebook's output feeds a downstream dbt gold-layer stage
failureModes: Using notebooks for what is really a tested SQL modelling problem, losing dbt's version control and test framework for no benefit
Letting notebook logic and dbt logic both claim ownership of the same conform step, duplicating and diverging over time

nodes.label: Warehouse stored procedures
nodes.summary: Procedural T-SQL embedded directly in the Warehouse, with no external tooling or version-control framework.
nodes.detail: Stored procedures let a team write transformation logic directly in T-SQL inside the Warehouse, without adopting external tooling. This is a legitimate path for teams that don't want a Python-based external framework like dbt, but it forgoes dbt's built-in version control, automated testing, and lineage documentation unless the team builds equivalent tooling itself.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is the lowest-friction path for a T-SQL-only team with no interest in external tooling, but the tradeoff is real: none of dbt's testing, lineage, or ref()-based dependency graph comes for free.

inputs: Warehouse tables and the transformation logic to embed in T-SQL
processing: Write CREATE PROCEDURE definitions implementing the transformation steps
Schedule execution via a pipeline or external scheduler
Maintain logic directly in the Warehouse with no separate project/version-control layer unless one is built manually
outputs: Transformed warehouse tables, produced by procedural T-SQL with no dbt-style lineage graph
drill.example: A team with an existing library of SQL Server stored procedures ports them largely as-is into the Warehouse rather than rewriting the same logic as dbt models, accepting the loss of dbt's dependency graph in exchange for not adopting new tooling.
controls: Manual version control (e.g. checking procedure DDL into git) since none is built in
failureModes: No automated testing framework, so regressions in a procedure surface only in downstream reports
Procedure dependency order becoming implicit and undocumented as the number of procedures grows

nodes.label: Warning: Fabric Warehouse's T-SQL surface is not SQL Server's
nodes.summary: dbt-fabric works around unsupported ALTER/MERGE/TRUNCATE by generating CTAS + DROP/CREATE instead.
nodes.detail: Fabric Data Warehouse's T-SQL surface does not support the same command set as SQL Server. The dbt-fabric adapter implements operations dbt models rely on — behaviors equivalent to ALTER TABLE ADD/ALTER/DROP COLUMN, MERGE, TRUNCATE, and sp_rename — by translating them into CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) plus DROP/CREATE sequences. dbt projects targeting Fabric Warehouse are subject to the same platform-wide T-SQL command and data-type limitations that apply outside of dbt; these are not adapter-specific restrictions.
nodes.whyItMatters: A team porting an existing dbt project or a stored-procedure library from SQL Server can hit this silently: schema-evolution operations that were cheap in-place ALTERs become full-table rebuild events in Fabric Warehouse, with real cost and downtime implications that only show up once the migration is underway.

evidence.note: The dbt-fabric adapter implements T-SQL operations dbt relies on — equivalent to ALTER TABLE ADD/ALTER/DROP COLUMN, MERGE, TRUNCATE, and sp_rename — by translating them into CTAS plus DROP/CREATE sequences, because Fabric Warehouse's T-SQL surface does not support the same command set as SQL Server.

dbt projects targeting Fabric Warehouse are subject to Fabric's general T-SQL command limitations and unsupported data types for tables — the same platform-wide constraints that apply outside of dbt, not adapter-specific restrictions.

inputs: A dbt project or stored-procedure library authored against, or ported from, full SQL Server semantics
processing: Audit model/procedure SQL and seed/data types against Fabric Warehouse's documented T-SQL surface before migration
Expect schema-evolution changes to run as rebuild-style DDL (CTAS + DROP/CREATE) rather than in-place ALTER
Treat model or procedure contract changes as full-table events for capacity and downtime planning
outputs: Models/procedures validated against Fabric's actual T-SQL and data-type surface before they hit production
drill.example: A dbt model that adds a nullable column via what would be a cheap ALTER TABLE on SQL Server instead triggers a full CTAS rebuild of the table under dbt-fabric, which the team only discovers when a routine schema change takes materially longer than expected on a large fact table.
controls: Validate SQL Server-specific types/commands against Fabric's documented T-SQL surface before migration, not after
Plan capacity and maintenance windows around rebuild-style DDL for schema changes
failureModes: Porting a SQL Server dbt project or procedure library assuming full ALTER/MERGE parity and discovering the gap in production
Underestimating migration effort because the surface gap is invisible until a schema-evolving model actually runs

nodes.label: Warning: splitting one transformation layer across tools
nodes.summary: Half the logic in a dataflow dbt can't see erases the lineage and testing benefits dbt exists to provide.
nodes.detail: A common composite pattern works well: ingest with pipelines/Dataflow Gen2, do heavy or non-tabular work in notebooks, and let dbt own the modeled, tested semantic-ready layer inside the Warehouse. The failure mode is splitting one logical transformation layer — not distinct stages, but the same modelling responsibility — across two of these tools, so that dbt's lineage graph and test suite only see half the actual data flow.
nodes.whyItMatters: The value of dbt's version control, testing, and lineage documentation depends on it seeing the whole modelling layer; once half the logic lives in a dataflow or notebook outside its dependency graph, that value silently evaporates while the team still believes they have full lineage and test coverage.

inputs: A transformation layer that grows over time across multiple tools without an explicit ownership boundary
processing: Draw an explicit boundary: pipelines/Dataflow Gen2 for ingestion, notebooks for non-tabular/lake-side work, dbt for the modelled, tested, version-controlled layer
Audit for logic that has drifted into the wrong surface (e.g. modelling joins added to a dataflow instead of a dbt model)
Migrate stray logic back into the surface that owns that responsibility
outputs: A transformation layer where each tool's boundary matches its actual responsibility, and dbt's lineage graph reflects the true data flow
drill.example: A team adds a business-logic join directly inside a Dataflow Gen2 step because it was convenient, while the rest of the star schema is built in dbt models; a later audit finds dbt's lineage graph and tests never covered that join, and a silent data-quality bug in it went undetected for months.
controls: Explicit, documented ownership boundary between ingestion, lake-side transformation, and warehouse modelling
Periodic lineage audits comparing the tool boundary against where logic actually lives
failureModes: Modelling logic quietly migrating into a dataflow or notebook over time, outside dbt's test and lineage coverage
Teams believing they have full lineage/test coverage because dbt reports clean, while untested logic lives elsewhere

walkthrough.title: 1. Name the kind of work first
walkthrough.explanation: Version-controlled SQL modelling, low-code shaping, Spark-shaped work, and embedded T-SQL are four different jobs before they're four different tools.

walkthrough.title: 2. dbt: tested, version-controlled modelling in the Warehouse
walkthrough.explanation: Reached through the third-party dbt-fabric adapter, not a native Fabric feature — the right choice when tests, lineage, and code review on the modelled layer matter.

walkthrough.title: 3. Dataflow Gen2: low-code shaping for analysts
walkthrough.explanation: Strongest for connector breadth and landing data into Fabric, weak for owning a large interdependent transformation codebase.

walkthrough.title: 4. Notebooks: Python/Spark and non-tabular work
walkthrough.explanation: The surface for unstructured data and ML feature engineering — work SQL-only dbt models can't express.

walkthrough.title: 5. Stored procedures: T-SQL with no external tooling
walkthrough.explanation: A legitimate path for T-SQL-only teams, at the cost of dbt's built-in version control, tests, and lineage.

walkthrough.title: 6. Warning: Fabric's T-SQL surface isn't SQL Server's
walkthrough.explanation: Both dbt-fabric and hand-written procedures inherit the same command and data-type limits — dbt-fabric compensates for missing ALTER/MERGE with CTAS plus DROP/CREATE, which changes the cost of schema evolution.

walkthrough.title: 7. Warning: don't split one layer across tools
walkthrough.explanation: Ingest with pipelines/Dataflow Gen2, do lake-side work in notebooks, let dbt own the modelled layer — but if modelling logic leaks into a dataflow or notebook, dbt's lineage and tests silently stop covering the whole picture.
